title: Allan pledges new laws to restrict AI in recruitment
full_text:
The Allan government has vowed to introduce the toughest workplace surveillance laws in the nation if it is re-elected, as it seeks to take on big tech and centre its campaign pitch on workers’ rights ahead of the November election.
Premier Jacinta Allan on Monday announced Labor would ban inappropriate monitoring of employees and bolster human oversight of artificial intelligence used during staff recruitment, amid growing community anxiety about AI.
“Victorian workers are living in a period of enormous change, and while a lot of this technological change and the use of AI can have some positive impacts on our daily lives, I hear from too many Victorians about their worries and concerns about the impact of technology and AI is having on them,” Allan said.
If re-elected, Labor would amend the Equal Opportunity Act to prevent AI bias during the recruitment process that it says can “systematically disadvantage women and people from diverse backgrounds”, and introduce a new standalone bill modelled on workplace surveillance laws in NSW and the Australian Capital Territory.
Employers who want to introduce or change their surveillance techniques would need to provide 14 days’ notice and open up a consultation period with their workforce.
They would also be prohibited from selling any workplace surveillance data, restricted from monitoring staff covertly unless for safety purposes (such as in prisons), and would need automated decisions to be reviewed by humans.
Victorian Trades Hall Council secretary Luke Hilakari said 80 per cent of its members who responded to a survey said they were being monitored in their workplaces. He cited one unnamed Victorian-based company that had secretly turned on the recording devices on the laptops of their workers while they were at home.
“Private conversations, kids playing in the background – all of that was recorded,” Hilakari said. “When the workers complained to their boss, they were sacked that week. So this [proposed law] needs to fill that gap.”
Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Sally Curtain said workplace discrimination and surveillance laws were already covered under the federal Fair Work Act, and any further changes by the state needed to be developed in a measured and technologically agnostic way.
“Employers need to be able to access the tools they require in order to comply with the suite of new legislative and regulatory requirements that the state and the federal governments have imposed on them,” Curtain said.
“Harmonisation between jurisdictions is absolutely critical rather than a siloed and haphazard approach.”
In a speech to a business conference late last year, Allan vowed to be ruthless about attracting more data centres to Victoria and aimed to position the state as the national leader in building the infrastructure that powers AI.
She announced a $5.5 million commitment for a Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan and $8.1 million to train white-collar workers in AI.
Community concern
But local communities are growing increasingly concerned about the infrastructure, while workers are anxious about the impact of the technology on their jobs and the economy.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week unveiled a more interventionist approach to AI, reflecting the scale of disruption the technology is causing.
Australia ranked equal lowest for AI sentiment, according to EY’s latest Global AI Sentiment Study released in May. A survey by the federal Office of the Information Commissioner released the same month found that only 4 per cent of Australians said they trusted their private information with AI companies.
Allan’s proposed laws are part of Labor’s plan to win back workers who may have abandoned the party in favour of One Nation, and come after the government last year announced it would legislate the right for all employees to work from home at least two days a week.
Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Victorians had a right to privacy. “We think there needs to be common sense ... but we’ll wait to see any legislation,” she said.
Labor is fighting to win a historic fourth term on November 28 as it faces a two-pronged threat from the Coalition and One Nation.
The latest The Australian Financial Review/Redbridge/Accent Research survey of 5516 Victorians, conducted between June 17 and June 28, showed Labor and the Coalition were neck and neck on a primary vote of 26 per cent each, while One Nation recorded a primary vote of 27 per cent.
A separate poll by Redbridge for Trades Hall revealed Labor would win 35 seats, the Coalition 39, One Nation 12 and the Greens two in a median-case scenario in the 88-seat lower house.
